title: The Transmission Mechanism of Climate Change Risk to Bank Stability: The Role of Economic Policy Uncertainty
content: This study examines the transmission mechanisms through which climate change risk influences bank financial stability in emerging economies, with particular emphasis on the role of economic policy uncertainty (EPU). Using annual panel data for 36 African countries over the period 2000–2020, the study employs panel data techniques with Driscoll–Kraay standard errors, with robustness assessed using the System Generalised Method of Moments with Instrumental Variables (System GMM-IV). The findings indicate that transition climate change risk, proxied by carbon emissions, is positively associated with bank financial stability, whereas the effect of physical climate change risk is negligible. The positive association between carbon emissions and bank stability is interpreted within the context of Africa’s ongoing industrialisation and relatively limited adoption of alternative clean-energy sources, rather than as evidence of a beneficial effect of carbon emissions on financial stability. Furthermore, EPU partially mediates the relationship between transition climate change risk and bank financial stability, while its mediating role is not supported for physical climate change risk. The findings also suggest that African banks exhibit risk-averse behaviour during periods of heightened economic uncertainty, with EPU exerting a direct effect on bank financial stability. However, the mediation results are sensitive to the treatment of dynamic dependence and endogeneity, as the mediating effect is not preserved under the System GMM-IV specification. These findings underscore the importance of accelerating the transition towards low-carbon energy sources while adopting integrated policy frameworks that enhance financial resilience as African economies continue to industrialise.
